compliance.notes: Strong core compliance (23 of 24 core requirements score >=2). Standout strengths: an exemplary liability benchmark charted separately for the General Fund and HRA out to ~2095 with all four balances (LB-01/02/04), a fully reconciled CFR (PI-02), an SLY-driven counterparty matrix using CDS beyond ratings (INV-01/03), a full-Council MRP policy with the VRP position disclosed (MRP-02), an integrated two-pool borrowing strategy (BOR-01) and a genuinely strategic capital strategy with proportionality analysis (CS-01). The single core gap is RISK-02 (interest-rate exposure) scored 1 - a qualitative interest-rate strategy and maturity-structure limits exist but no explicit fixed-vs-variable exposure limits are set. Other notable weaknesses: treasury scrutiny is assigned to the Cabinet/executive rather than an independent committee (GOV-04); no treasury ESG policy (ESG-01, 0); no audit-qualification flag (RPT-05, 0) or MRP-in-accounts disclosure (MRP-03, 0) in the scored documents; no explicit monetary cap on loans to external bodies (COM-09); and no MiFID II status disclosure (INV-07). The document sits within a severely stressed budget (Exceptional Financial Support reliance, among the lowest reserves of any UA, S114 risk if EFS refused), which the strategy reflects but does not fully stress-test for affordability.

gaps.evidence: cover report §12.3 p.18 the Capital Strategy and TMSS are 'compliant with the new code and do not include capital investment activity where the primary purpose is commercial yield'; Capital Strategy(App5) §1.4/§5.4

Capital Strategy(App5) §7.6 p.10 'No overall cap has been set on the total loan value that may be provided to external bodies. Each loan is considered on its own merits'; no aggregate service/commercial investment limit stated

TMSS(App6) §4.4.1/§4.4.4 pp.19-20 pooled funds addressed (money market funds and ultra/short-dated bond funds with limits; Royal London bond funds in §4.1.1 p.16); no MiFID II professional-client status disclosure found in either document
TMSS(App6) §4.2(xi) p.18 and §4.4.1 p.19 all investments sterling-denominated; borrowing is PWLB/market/LA (sterling) but no explicit sterling-only borrowing statement

news_drafts.headline: Brighton and Hove asks government for up to £30m of exceptional support for 2026/27 overspend
news_drafts.lead:
Brighton and Hove City Council has asked the government for exceptional financial support (permission to borrow, or sell assets, to cover day-to-day spending, a last resort) of up to £30m for 2026/27. The request is set out in the council's budget monitoring report for August, the fifth month of the financial year, which goes to its Cabinet on 15 October.

The council says the request follows its reported financial position, which includes a forecast overspend (where a council expects to end the year having spent more than it budgeted). It has approached the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. The papers describe it as a request for "more" support for the year.

The report says plainly what the money is: "this is additional borrowing, not additional funding." The council states that it provides a one-year easing of the position, but that repaying it adds cost to future years' budgets.

news_drafts.headline: Brighton and Hove faces £20.9m overspend, requests £30m government loan
news_drafts.lead: Brighton and Hove Council is requesting permission from government to borrow an additional £30m — known as exceptional financial support — after forecasting a £20.852m overspend for 2026/27. The council has warned that if the request is denied, its chief finance officer will file a Section 114 notice, a formal warning that the council cannot balance its budget from income. The overspend stems from three main pressures: temporary accommodation (£12m), adult social care placements (£12m), and schools funding for special educational needs (£8.925m). The council's transformation programmes are on track but cannot keep pace with rising demand and costs. A CIPFA review found financial resilience weaknesses; the council reports improvements are being implemented, with a follow-up assessment scheduled for end of September.

findings.headline: Commercial property rental income declined structurally with New England House closure reducing annual income by approximately £900k
findings.detail: Commercial rental income declined with the closure of New England House reducing income by approximately £900k, compounded by disposals of properties to achieve capital receipts, void properties, and rent reductions from lease renewals. The Central Hub Property Services budget shows a £0.999m pressure from lost rental income and vacant property costs.
findings.matters: The council is not replacing lost income from strategic property disposals, creating a structural revenue loss that must be offset by budget cuts or new income generation elsewhere.
findings.figures: New England House closure ~£900k annual loss; Property Services pressure £0.999m; Central Hub overspend £0.910m (2.97%)
findings.quote: 2025/26 saw the closure of New England House reducing the commercial income generated by c.£900k. Other factors for the reduced income relates to the disposal of properties to achieve a capital receipt, void properties or rent reductions as a consequence or lease renewals or new lettings.

findings.headline: Pupils transported by taxi increased 57% since 2022/23 with average costs up 53% over same period
findings.detail: Home-to-school transport by taxi has grown 57% in pupil numbers and 53% in average cost per pupil since 2022/23, reflecting increased demand (likely including SEND pupils) and volatile taxi market pricing. The service is managing costs through personal travel budgets and route reviews, but underlying growth continues to drive pressure.
findings.matters: Demand-driven cost growth in pupil transport parallels EHCP and children in care growth, signalling strong underlying demand pressures across children's services that other councils are also experiencing.
findings.figures: 57% increase in pupils transported since 2022/23; 53% increase in average cost; forecast overspend £0.447m (1.53% of budget)
findings.quote: Since the beginning of the 2022/23 financial year there has been an increase of 57% in the number of pupils transported by taxi and a 53% increase in the average cost.

findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation demand increased significantly in August 2026/27 after four months of reduction, increasing costs above forecast assumptions
findings.detail: TA demand reduced during the first four months of 2026/27 but spiked significantly in August, reversing the downward trend and increasing costs above forecast. Current accommodation pressures are £2.171m, partially offset by forecast savings of £1.636m from the recovery plan. Delays to transformation initiatives (Dynamic Market, Base One, Exempt Accommodation, EPC) are creating delivery risk to the planned savings.
findings.matters: The TA recovery plan depends critically on keeping demand suppressed; the August spike shows demand remains volatile and the plan's assumptions may not hold, putting forecast savings at risk.
findings.figures: Accommodation pressures £2.171m; forecast recovery savings £1.636m; net forecast overspend £0.535m (3.65% of budget)
findings.quote: Whilst demand reduced during the first four months of the year, August saw a significant increase in households requiring TA, reversing the previous downward trend and increasing accommodation costs above forecast assumptions.

findings.headline: Organisational Transformation programme has not delivered £1.125m of planned central savings, with cross-cutting programme delayed
findings.detail: The council's centrally-held budget overspend increased £1.729m at month 5, driven principally by £1.125m non-delivery of Organisational Transformation savings. Whilst organisational change has occurred in areas already identified by services, the cross-cutting transformation programme has experienced delays.
findings.matters: If the flagship transformation programme is delivering only locally-identified changes rather than cross-cutting savings, finance directors question whether it can successfully deliver the service redesigns needed to manage structural demand pressures.
findings.figures: Centrally-held budget overspend increase £1.729m at month 5; Organisational Transformation savings not delivered £1.125m
findings.quote: Whilst headway has been made in delivering organisational change, this has been in areas that were already identified by services. There has been some delay in delivery of the cross-cutting programme.

findings.headline: Children with Education, Health and Care Plans increasing 12% per annum with high needs block allocation at cash flat funding
findings.detail: EHCP numbers have more than doubled between 2016 and 2025 and continue to increase at 12% per year, with rising complexity of need driving higher unit costs. However, the high needs block allocation for 2026/27 is cash flat—no uplift for growth or inflation. The high needs block is forecast to overspend by £7.797m (18.06% of budget).
findings.matters: Demand growth at 12% per annum significantly exceeds funding growth at 0%, creating a structural deficit that must be addressed through service redesign or eventually through reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: EHCP numbers more than doubled 2016-2025; 12% per year current growth; high needs block overspend £7.797m (18.06% of budget); cash flat funding
findings.quote: the number of children with Education, Health and Care plans are continuing to go up by 12% per year, whilst unit costs are also increasing. The high needs block allocation received in 2026/27 is at a cash flat level with no uplift provided for growth or inflation factors.
